channel.title: AI Stupa Translation Project
channel.description: New English translations of texts from the Tibetan Buddhist canon, made by the AI Stupa (provisional, public domain).

item.title: An Explanation of the Eight Charnel Grounds (Toh 1216)
item.description: An Explanation of the Eight Charnel Grounds, known in Sanskrit as the Aṣṭaśmaśānākhyāta, is a short tantric work that describes the eight great charnel grounds, the cremation sites that ring the protective circle of many tantric maṇḍalas. Opening with homage to the Blessed One Lokeśvara, it moves through each direction in turn, naming each charnel ground, such as Caṇḍogra in the east and Gahvara…

item.title: The Means of Accomplishment of Glorious Hevajra (Toh 1218)
item.description: The Means of Accomplishment of Glorious Hevajra, known in Sanskrit as Śrī Hevajra Sādhana and in Tibetan as Dpal dgyes pa rdo rje'i sgrub thabs, is a tantric meditation manual devoted to the deity Hevajra and his consort Nairātmyā. Opening with a verse of homage to the two deities and an acknowledgment of the kindness of the vajra master, it sets out the ritual procedure by which a practitioner…

item.title: The Rite of the Sequence of Activities for the Hevajra Maṇḍala (Toh 1219)
item.description: The Rite of the Sequence of Activities for the Hevajra Maṇḍala, known in Sanskrit as the Hevajra Maṇḍala Karma Krama Vidhi and in Tibetan as Kye rdo rje'i dkyil 'khor gyi las kyi rim pa'i cho ga, is a ritual manual belonging to the Hevajra cycle of tantric practice. After paying homage to the glorious Hevajra, it explains how a qualified master, one who has received empowerment from his own guru…

item.title: The Pith Instruction of Glorious Hevajra Like the Tip of a Lamp Flame (Toh 1220)
item.description: The Instruction of Glorious Hevajra Like the Tip of a Lamp Flame, known in Sanskrit as Śrī Hevajra Pradīpa Śūlopama Avavādaka and in Tibetan by a title beginning Dpal gyi rdo rje'i mar me'i rtse mo lta bu'i, is a short tantric pith instruction on the practice of Hevajra. Opening with homage to Hevajra and to the goddess Nairātmyā, the author presents teachings received from the master…

item.title: The Rite of the Hevajra Maṇḍala (Toh 1221)
item.description: The Rite of the Hevajra Maṇḍala, known in Sanskrit as the Hevajra Maṇḍala Vidhi and in Tibetan as Gyepa Dorjé Maṇḍal gyi Choga, is a short ritual manual for the practice centered on the deity Hevajra, a principal figure of the highest class of Buddhist tantra. After paying homage to glorious Heruka, it guides the practitioner through the preliminary steps of the maṇḍala rite. These include…

item.title: Toh 1222 (Toh 1222)
item.description: This text, Toh 1222 in the Tengyur, is a short verse hymn of praise to Hevajra, the wrathful tantric deity also invoked here as Heruka. Its Tibetan title, which survives only in fragmentary form in the source and opens with the word thams, meaning "all," cannot be fully reconstructed, so no reliable English or Sanskrit title can be given. The hymn honors Hevajra as the supreme intrinsic nature of…

item.title: The Great King of Tantras Called Glorious Vajraḍāka (Toh 370)
item.description: The Great King of Tantras called Glorious Vajraḍāka, known in Sanskrit as Śrī Vajraḍāka Nāma Mahātantrarāja and in Tibetan as Gyü kyi Gyalpo Chenpo Pal Dorjé Khandro, is a major esoteric scripture centered on the deity Vajraḍāka. After an homage to the noble Avalokiteśvara, the Great Compassionate One, it praises Vajraḍāka as the self-arisen Blessed One and the very reality of all ḍākas, a deity…

item.title: Explanation of the Sixty-Four Daṇḍas (Toh 1210)
item.description: The Explanation of the Sixty-Four Daṇḍas, known in Tibetan as dbyu gu drug cu rtsa bzhi'i bshad pa, is a short technical treatise on reckoning time, where a daṇḍa is a traditional Indian unit of time equivalent to a water-clock period. It defines the daṇḍas by counting breaths, five thousand four hundred in half a day and twenty-one thousand six hundred in a full day and night, with three hundred…

item.title: The Analysis of the Reality of Hevajra (Toh 1211)
item.description: The Analysis of the Reality of Hevajra, known in Tibetan as Kye rdo rje'i de kho na nyid rnam par phye ba, is a short tantric work that explains the inner meaning of the iconography of Hevajra, a principal deity of the Highest Yoga Tantra tradition. In verse, it interprets the deity's sixteen hands as the sixteen emptinesses. It also reads the animals held in his skull cups as symbols: the…

item.title: The Eight Charnel Grounds (Toh 1212)
item.description: The Eight Charnel Grounds, known in Sanskrit as Aṣṭaśmaśāna and in Tibetan as Dur khrod brgyad, is a short tantric work that opens with homage to Hevajra and sets out the features of the eight charnel grounds that surround a deity's mandala. For each direction, beginning in the east, it lists the field's sacred tree, the name of the charnel ground, the world protector who guards it, the nāga king…

item.title: The Eight Charnel Grounds (Toh 1213)
item.description: The Eight Charnel Grounds, known in Sanskrit as Aṣṭaśmaśāna and in Tibetan as Dur khrod brgyad, is a short versified work in the tantric tradition of the deity Heruka. After paying homage to the guru as the glorious hero Heruka, who bestows both enjoyment and liberation, the author explains that he is writing as an aid to his own memory. He records the names and directional placement of the eight…

item.title: Ascertaining the Signs (Toh 1214)
item.description: Ascertaining the Signs, known in Tibetan as Brda nges par gzung ba, is a short tantric treatise that opens with homage to glorious Hevajra and explains how practitioners should understand the secret signs used within the Hevajra tradition. Its Sanskrit title is not given in the opening lines. The work teaches that these signs should be understood first by their literal sound and then according to…

item.title: The Determination of the Sites and So Forth (Toh 1215)
item.description: The Determination of the Sites and So Forth, known in Sanskrit as the Pīṭhādinirṇaya and in Tibetan as gnas la sogs pa gtan la dbab pa, is a short tantric treatise that opens with homage to glorious Hevajra and to the lotus feet of Vajrayoginī. Its author promises to write concisely and clearly, and the work explains a passage from the Hevajra Tantra, the scripture known as the Two Examinations…

item.title: The Praise in One Hundred and Fifty Verses (Toh 1147)
item.description: The Praise Called the One Hundred and Fifty, known in Sanskrit as the Śatapañcāśatka and in Tibetan as Brgya lnga bcu pa zhes bya ba'i bstod pa, is a devotional hymn in verse addressed to the Buddha and traditionally attributed to the Indian poet Mātṛceṭa. Opening with homage to the Three Jewels, it extols the Buddha as the one in whom every fault is absent and every good quality is complete, and…

item.title: Verses in Praise of the Gaṇḍī (Toh 1149)
item.description: Verses in Praise of the Gaṇḍī, known in Sanskrit as the Gaṇḍīstotragāthā and in Tibetan as Gaṇḍī'i bstod pa tshigs su bcad pa, is a devotional hymn honoring the gaṇḍī, the wooden gong struck to summon the monastic community. Opening with homage to the Buddha, the poem recalls his awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, where armored hosts and alluring women advanced on him with clamorous shouts and…

item.title: The Interwoven Praise (Toh 1150)
item.description: The Interwoven Praise, known in Sanskrit as the Miśrakastotra and in Tibetan as Spel mar bstod pa, is a devotional hymn addressed to the Buddha as the Omniscient One. It opens with the voice of someone sinking in the bottomless ocean of saṃsāra, devoured by the sea monsters of attachment and the other afflictions, who asks to whom they should turn for refuge, whose teaching they should follow…

item.title: Praise to All the Tathāgatas (Toh 1151)
item.description: The Praise to All the Tathāgatas, known in Sanskrit as the Sarvatathāgata Stotra and in Tibetan as De bzhin gshegs pa thams cad la bstod pa, is a short devotional hymn addressed collectively to all the buddhas. Opening with homage to the Three Jewels, it unfolds in verses that each close with the same refrain of bowing to all the Tathāgatas, celebrating their supreme teaching, their skill in…

item.title: A Praise of the Blessed One Śākyamuni (Toh 1152)
item.description: A Praise of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, known in Sanskrit as Bhagavān Śākyamuni Stotra and in Tibetan as Bcom ldan 'das shākya thub pa'i bstod pa, is a short devotional hymn in verse addressed to the historical Buddha. After an homage to the Three Jewels, it extols Śākyamuni as the lamp and illuminator of the world, one who has passed beyond worldly existence yet works tirelessly for the benefit…

item.title: Praise of the Glorious Venerable Mahābodhi (Toh 1153)
item.description: The Praise of the Glorious Venerable Mahābodhi, known in Tibetan as Dpal ldan rje btsun byang chub chen po'i bstod pa, carries a Sanskrit title preserved in a somewhat irregular form that approximates Śrīmanmahābodhibhaṭṭāraka Stotra. It is a devotional hymn addressed to the Buddha Śākyamuni, honored here as the "Great Awakening," and it begins with a homage to the Buddha. Its verses praise him…

item.title: A Praise of the Buddha in Ten Verses (Toh 1154)
item.description: A Praise of the Buddha in Ten Verses, whose Sanskrit title appears in the translation as Buddhastavadaśa, is a short devotional hymn addressed to the Buddha Śākyamuni. In a series of verses, each ending with a refrain of homage, it celebrates his first arousing of the aspiration for supreme awakening, his attainment of deathless liberation for the benefit of beings, his victory over Māra, and his…

item.title: The Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Hevajra Tantra (Toh 1181)
item.description: The Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Hevajra Tantra, called Padminī, known in Sanskrit as the Hevajratantrapañjikā Padminī and in Tibetan as Kye'i rdo rje'i rgyud kyi dka' 'grel padma can, is an Indian commentary on the Hevajra Tantra, one of the principal scriptures of the highest class of Buddhist tantra. It opens with homage to Mañjuśrī, to Vajrasattva as lord of the ḍākinīs, and to…

item.title: The Expansion of Reality: A Commentary on the Difficult Points of the King of Tantras, the Ḍākinī Vajra Net (Toh 1196)
item.description: This work is A Commentary on the Difficult Points of the King of Tantras, the Ḍākinī Vajra Net, called The Expansion of Reality, known in Sanskrit as the Ḍākinīvajrapañjaratantrarājasya Tattvapauṣṭikapañjikā and in Tibetan as Rgyud kyi rgyal po mkha' 'gro ma rdo rje dra ba'i dka' 'grel de kho na nyid rgyas pa. It is a pañjikā, an explanatory commentary that clarifies difficult passages of a root…

item.title: The Reality of Song (Toh 1207)
item.description: The Reality of Song, known in Sanskrit as the Gītitattva, is a short tantric commentary that opens with homage to glorious Hevajra and explains, word by word, the hidden meaning of a vernacular song associated with the Hevajra tradition. Taking each phrase of the song in turn, it reads its seemingly ordinary words as references to yogic experience, such as the unfabricated awakening mind, the…

item.title: Commentary on the Vajra Song (Toh 1208)
item.description: The Commentary on the Vajra Song, known in Sanskrit as the Vajragītibhāṣya and in Tibetan as Dorjé Lu Shepa, is a short tantric commentary that explains the meaning of a vajra song, an esoteric verse in the Apabhraṃśa language of the kind sung by practitioners at tantric gatherings. After paying homage to the holy guru, to the heroes and heroines who dwell in the sacred sites and fields, and to…

item.title: The Stages of Clear Realization (Toh 1209)
item.description: The Stages of Clear Realization, known in Sanskrit as the Abhisamayakrama and in Tibetan as Ngönpar Tokpé Rimpa, is a short tantric treatise devoted to the meditative practice of the Hevajra Tantra. Opening with homage to glorious Hevajra, it presents itself as a teaching on the precious clear realization of that tantra, which is said to have come from glorious Uḍḍiyāna. Its opening passages turn…

item.title: Verses of Auspiciousness of the Seven Buddhas (Toh 1104)
item.description: This short work can be called in English the Verses of Auspiciousness of the Seven Buddhas. Its Sanskrit and Tibetan titles are not given in the opening lines supplied here. After a homage to the Three Jewels, it moves through a sequence of benedictory stanzas, each recalling one of the buddhas of the past, beginning with Vipaśyin, Śikhin, and Viśvabhū. For each, it notes his caste, the human…

item.title: Auspicious Verses of the Five Tathāgatas (Toh 1105)
item.description: The Auspicious Verses of the Five Tathāgatas, known in Sanskrit as the Pañcatathāgatamaṅgalagāthā and in Tibetan as De bzhin gshegs pa lnga'i bkra shis tshigs su bcad pa, is a short devotional poem of blessing addressed to the five buddhas of the tantric tradition. After an opening homage to the Three Jewels, it praises each tathāgata in turn, beginning with Vairocana and Akṣobhya and continuing…

item.title: The Auspiciousness of the Three Families (Toh 1106)
item.description: The Auspiciousness of the Three Families, known in Sanskrit as Trikulamaṅgala and in Tibetan as Rigs gsum gyi bkra shis, is a brief verse prayer of benediction addressed to the three great protector bodhisattvas. After an opening homage to the Three Jewels, it invokes Mañjuśrī, golden like a king of mountains, as the embodiment of the enlightened body; Avalokiteśvara, white as a conch, as the…

item.title: An Auspicious Praise of the Three Jewels (Toh 1139)
item.description: An Auspicious Praise of the Three Jewels, known in Sanskrit as the Triratnamaṅgalastotra and in Tibetan by a title of the same meaning that begins with dkon mchog, the word for the Jewels, is a devotional hymn honoring the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Opening with homage to the Three Jewels, it praises the Buddha in rich, lyrical verse as a sage with a golden hue, lotus-like eyes, and a…

item.title: Praise of the Marks of the Perfectly Awakened Buddha (Toh 1140)
item.description: The Praise of the Marks of the Perfectly Awakened Buddha, known in Sanskrit as the Samyaksambuddhalakṣaṇastotra, is a devotional hymn that celebrates the physical perfection of the Buddha. After an homage to the Three Jewels, it honors the Blessed One as the jewel of Śuddhodana's lineage, worshipped by gods and asuras, and then describes his body feature by feature in rich verse. Soft black…

item.title: The Praise Ascending from One (Toh 1141)
item.description: The Praise Ascending from One, known in Sanskrit as the Ekottarikastava and in Tibetan as gcig las 'phros pa'i bstod pa, is a short devotional hymn addressed to the Buddha. After an opening homage to the noble Mañjuśrī, it unfolds through a numerical sequence of verses, each built around an ascending number: the one Dharma and the single eye of the world, the two truths, the three concentrations…

item.title: Praise of the Thirty-Five Sugatas, a Garland of Precious Names (Toh 1142)
item.description: The Praise of the Thirty-Five Sugatas, Adorned with Their Precious Names, known in Sanskrit as the Sugatapañcatriṃśatratnanāmamālāstotra, is a devotional hymn in verse honoring the thirty-five buddhas traditionally invoked in practices of confession and purification. After opening with homage and refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, it devotes a verse to each buddha in turn. It begins with…

item.title: Praise in Eight Verses (Toh 1143)
item.description: The Praise in Eight Verses, whose Sanskrit title is given in the translation as Padasya Aṣṭakastotra, is a short devotional hymn of homage in eight stanzas. After an opening salutation to Mañjuśrī in youthful form, it extols the Buddha through vivid similes: a face like the full moon, a voice like a lion's roar, the strength of an elephant, and a mind as steadfast as the king of mountains and as…

item.title: A Praise of the Three Jewels (Toh 1144)
item.description: A Praise of the Three Jewels, known in Sanskrit as the Triratnastotra and in Tibetan as Dkon mchog gsum gyi bstod pa, is a short devotional hymn that pays homage in turn to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. It opens with a simple verse of salutation to all three and then praises each more fully. The Buddha is honored as one who has perfected the two great accumulations, attained the four…

item.title: Commentary on the Praise of the Three Jewels (Toh 1145)
item.description: The Commentary on the Praise of the Three Jewels, known in Sanskrit as the Triratnastotravṛtti and in Tibetan as Dkon mchog gsum la bstod pa'i 'grel pa, is a short explanatory treatise on a hymn of praise to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Opening with homage to Mañjuśrī in youthful form, it explains that honoring the Three Jewels, the gurus of the threefold existence, is the cause of…

item.title: A Praise of the Three Jewels (Toh 1146)
item.description: A Praise of the Three Jewels, known in Sanskrit as the Triratna Stotra and in Tibetan as Könchok Sum gyi Töpa, is a brief devotional hymn attributed in its closing line to the master Vasubandhu. In three short verses, it pays homage in turn to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. The Buddha is honored through his three bodies: the dharmakāya beyond all reference, the sambhogakāya of perfect…

item.title: Praise of the Glorious Goddess Sarasvatī (Toh 1092)
item.description: Praise of the Glorious Goddess Sarasvatī, known in Tibetan as Pal Lhamo Drayang la Töpa, is a short devotional hymn addressed to Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech, learning, and eloquence, whom Tibetans call Yangchenma or Drayangma. It opens by taking refuge in the many maṇḍalas of wisdom through which the buddhas arise and the bodhisattva grounds unfold. It then praises Sarasvatī as a sage who…

item.title: The Noble Great Sūtra on Entering the City of Vaiśālī (Toh 1093)
item.description: The Noble Great Sūtra on Entering the City of Vaiśālī, known in Sanskrit as the Āryavaiśālīpraveśamahāsūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Yangpé Drongkhyer du Jukpé Do Chenpo, is a short discourse set during the Buddha's travels through the land of the Vṛjis. After staying at a boatmen's lodging among the reeds, the Buddha comes to Āmrapālī's grove outside Vaiśālī and sends the venerable Ānanda into…

item.title: The Aspiration Found in the Ritual Manual of Noble Avalokiteśvara (Toh 1094)
item.description: The Aspiration Found in the Ritual Manual of Noble Avalokiteśvara, the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, known in Tibetan as Phakpa Chenrezik Wangchuk Yishin gyi Norbü Tokpa le Mönlam Jungwa, is a short aspiration prayer said to be drawn from a larger ritual manual devoted to Avalokiteśvara in his wish-fulfilling jewel form; no Sanskrit title is clearly attested for it. It opens with homage to the buddha…

item.title: The Noble King of Aspiration Prayers for Excellent Conduct (Toh 1095)
item.description: The Noble King of Aspiration Prayers for Excellent Conduct, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Bhadracaryāpraṇidhānarāja and in Tibetan as Pakpa Zangpo Chöpé Mönlam gyi Gyalpo, is one of the most beloved prayers in the Mahāyāna tradition. Written in verse and opening with homage to the youthful Mañjuśrī, it voices the bodhisattva's vast aspiration. It begins by bowing to all the buddhas of the three…

item.title: The Aspiration of Supreme Conduct (Toh 1097)
item.description: The Aspiration of Supreme Conduct, known in Sanskrit as Agracaryāpraṇidhāna and in Tibetan as Chokgi Chöpé Mönlam, is a short verse prayer of aspiration in the Mahāyāna tradition. It opens with an homage to all buddhas and bodhisattvas and bows to the buddhas of the ten directions for the benefit and happiness of all beings. It invokes Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and Dharmamati as models of how to pay…

item.title: The Jewel Verses (Toh 1098)
item.description: This short verse text, recorded in the Tibetan canon without a formal title and known by its theme as a discourse on the supreme jewels, is a poem of blessing and protection closely parallel to the Jewel Discourse, the Ratana Sutta of the Pali tradition, which is called the Ratnasūtra in Sanskrit. It opens with homage to the Three Jewels and then praises, verse by verse, the Buddha as the god of…

item.title: Toh 1099 (Toh 1099)
item.description: This short Kangyur text has no formal title of its own and is known by its opening words, "Homage to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones," in Tibetan Sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das rnams la phyag 'tshal. It is a brief verse prayer of auspiciousness and protection. It first recalls the seven buddhas of the past, from Vipaśyin through Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa to Śākyamuni…

item.title: Verses of Auspiciousness Requested by a God (Toh 1100)
item.description: Verses of Auspiciousness Requested by a God, known in Sanskrit as Devaparipṛcchāmaṅgalagāthā and in Tibetan as Lhas zhus pa'i bkra shis kyi tshigs su bcad pa, is a short verse text in which a god approaches the Buddha while he dwells in a solitary place and asks what the supreme auspiciousness is, since gods and humans each speak of auspicious things in their own way. In reply, the Buddha lists…

item.title: Verses of Well-Being (Toh 1101)
item.description: The Verses of Well-Being, known in Sanskrit as Svastigāthā and in Tibetan as Delek kyi Tsik su Chepa, is a brief verse text of blessing meant to be recited for auspiciousness and protection. It opens with a god approaching the Buddha and asking what words should be spoken so that well-being may arise, and the Buddha answers with a series of verses praising the Three Jewels as incomparable…

item.title: Verses for Well-Being (Toh 1102)
item.description: The Verses for Well-Being, known in Sanskrit as the Svastyayanagāthā and in Tibetan as Bde legs su 'gyur ba'i tshigs su bcad pa, is a brief scripture in verse that presents a dialogue between a god and the Buddha. The god approaches the Guide of the World and asks how one may always come to well-being, and the Buddha answers with a series of stanzas, each ending with the refrain that such people…

item.title: Verses of Auspiciousness (Toh 1103)
item.description: Verses of Auspiciousness, known in Sanskrit as Maṅgalagāthā and in Tibetan as Tashi kyi tsik su chepa, is a short work of benediction verses that celebrates the auspiciousness of the Three Jewels. After an opening homage, it praises the Buddha in turn as a golden mountain of excellence and protector of the three worlds, the sacred Dharma he taught as the supreme and unshakable virtue of the…

item.title: The King of Tantras (Toh 362)
item.description: The King of Tantras, the Glorious Kālacakra, Issued from the Supreme Primordial Buddha, known in Sanskrit as the Paramādibuddhoddhṛta Śrī Kālacakra Nāma Tantrarāja and in Tibetan as mchog gi dang po'i sangs rgyas las phyung ba rgyud kyi rgyal po dpal dus kyi 'khor lo, is the root scripture of the Kālacakra, or "Wheel of Time," tradition. It opens with King Sucandra bowing before the Buddha…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī That Saves the Preta Jvālāmukha (Toh 1080)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī That Saves the Preta Jvālāmukha, known in Tibetan as Yi dgas kha nas me 'bar ba la skyabs mdzad pa'i gzungs, is a short dhāraṇī scripture whose Sanskrit title is associated with the name of the flame-mouthed hungry ghost, Jvālāmukha. It opens with the Buddha teaching in Kapilavastu, while the venerable Ānanda, meditating alone at night, is confronted by a terrifying preta whose mouth…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī Called Obstructing Generosity (Toh 1081)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī Called Obstructing Generosity is a short scripture whose title is given only in Tibetan, with no Sanskrit title recorded, which suggests it may have been composed or compiled in Tibet rather than translated from an Indian original. After paying homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, it warns that obstructing the generosity of others brings consequences even worse than stinginess…
